paragraphs: Foundation models are pretrained on broad datasets and then adapted to particular tasks. This paper asks what makes a saved pretraining checkpoint a good starting point for that adaptation. The question concerns the checkpoint’s capacity to support later fine-tuning, including when the eventual task is not yet known.

The authors introduce downstream free energy, a Bayesian model selection criterion. It assesses adaptability through the concentration of nearby parameter settings that are favorable for a downstream task. The idea is to evaluate the neighborhood around a checkpoint: how much favorable parameter space is available near the starting model.

The authors show that the criterion can be implemented without downstream data or advance knowledge of the downstream task. They also report empirical evidence that its values reliably correlate with better fine-tuning performance. This makes the criterion a principled candidate for selecting checkpoints before adaptation begins. The stated evidence establishes a useful empirical relationship between the criterion and adaptability, rather than a guarantee that every selected checkpoint will perform best.
icml-2025-a-bayesian-model-selection-cri.tldr: Downstream free energy assesses a pretraining checkpoint’s adaptability without downstream data and empirically correlates with better fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Learning to defer lets a system decide which agent should handle an input. Existing two-stage approaches have mainly treated classification and regression separately. This paper develops a unified deferral mechanism for applications that require both kinds of prediction, so delegation can account for the combined task.

The method uses a family of surrogate losses: training objectives that stand in for the delegation objective. The authors prove Bayes consistency and consistency relative to the relevant function classes, establishing conditions connecting surrogate optimization to an optimal rejector, the component that decides when to defer. They also derive explicit bounds involving cross-entropy and agent-specific costs.

The analysis extends minimizability gaps to settings with multiple experts and makes explicit how shared representations affect the guarantees. This matters because multi-task models commonly share internal features across outputs. Experiments on object detection and electronic health record analysis demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and expose limitations of existing deferral methods in these multi-task settings. The contribution combines a practical delegation framework with theory that accounts for interactions between tasks.
icml-2025-a-two-stage-learning-to-defer-.tldr: A unified two-stage deferral framework handles classification and regression together, with consistency guarantees and supporting multi-task experiments.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a neural network is expected to handle. This paper develops a theoretical framework for constructing features specifically for that decision. Its focus is on explaining how useful detection features can arise from an explicit information-based objective.

The objective has two parts. A term based on KL divergence separates the feature distributions of familiar and unfamiliar inputs. An Information Bottleneck term favors compact features that preserve information relevant to detecting unfamiliar data. Together, these terms express a balance between distinguishing the two groups and compressing the representation. A variational optimization procedure produces features from this objective.

Under assumptions about out-of-distribution data, the framework recovers properties of existing feature-shaping functions. It also predicts a new shaping function that the authors report outperforms existing ones on OOD benchmarks. This connects established techniques and a new empirical result to the same theoretical construction. The recovery of existing properties depends on the stated distributional assumptions, while the performance claim concerns the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2025-a-variational-information-theo.tldr: An information-theoretic objective explains existing OOD features and yields a new feature-shaping function with stronger reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: A two-stage learning-to-defer system sends each input to a fixed main model or one of several offline experts. Its allocation decision is itself a potential attack target. Perturbed inputs can cause inappropriate delegation or concentrate requests on an expert, making routing robustness important alongside the quality of individual predictions.

The authors introduce two attack strategies. Untargeted attacks disrupt the preferred allocation, while targeted attacks push requests toward a particular agent. To defend against these threats, they propose SARD, a convex learning algorithm built around surrogate losses. These losses provide a tractable training objective for robust delegation.

The paper proves Bayes-consistency and function-class consistency guarantees for the proposed loss family across classification, regression, and multi-task settings. These results connect the training objective to the intended decision problem. Empirical evaluations show substantially improved robustness under adversarial attacks while preserving strong performance on clean inputs. Together, the attacks, algorithm, and guarantees establish a framework for studying how adversarial manipulation affects delegation, with the reported experiments supporting SARD’s defensive value.
icml-2025-adversarial-robustness-in-two-.tldr: SARD strengthens two-stage delegation against adversarial misrouting, with consistent surrogate losses and improved empirical robustness.

paragraphs: Online decision-making can pursue two goals: stay close to a trusted reference strategy and adapt toward whichever fixed strategy performs best over time. This paper asks whether one algorithm can provide strong guarantees for both goals when it receives bandit feedback, meaning feedback is limited to the action it chooses.

The authors give an affirmative answer when the reference strategy assigns positive probability to every action. Their algorithm guarantees O(1) regret relative to that comparator, while retaining approximately square-root-in-T regret relative to any fixed strategy. Here T is the number of rounds, and the second bound suppresses logarithmic factors. The full-support requirement is a stated condition of the result.

The authors apply the result to zero-sum games whose minimax value is zero, including normal-form and extensive-form games. In these settings, their approach can limit loss to O(1) while being able to obtain gains proportional to T against exploitable opponents. The significance is a formal combination of minimax-style protection and the ability to benefit from an opponent’s weaknesses.
icml-2025-best-of-both-worlds-regret-min.tldr: With a full-support comparator, bandit learning can combine constant regret against that reference with near-square-root regret against any fixed strategy.

paragraphs: Physical reasoning becomes difficult when objects interact in ways an agent does not already understand. Planning an entire solution in advance may be impractical because the consequences of an action are uncertain. This paper addresses tasks where an agent actively explores the environment and improves its choices through observed causes and effects.

Causal-PIK uses Bayesian optimization to guide the search for the next action. Its central component is a physics-informed kernel, which brings information about physical interactions into that search. The method connects reasoning about how actions affect objects with the optimization process used to choose subsequent attempts.

On the Virtual Tools and PHYRE benchmarks, the authors report better results than the state of the art, with fewer actions needed to reach the goal. They also compare the method with human studies, including a new study on PHYRE. Causal-PIK remains competitive on tasks that are difficult even for human participants. These findings support the value of incorporating physical structure into action search when interaction dynamics are unknown.
icml-2025-causal-pik-causality-based-phy.tldr: Causal-PIK combines Bayesian optimization with a physics-informed kernel to solve physical reasoning tasks using fewer actions.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning learns a reward function from human comparisons instead of requiring someone to specify rewards directly. This can help align behavior with human intentions, but comparisons become difficult when two behavior segments look similar. Unclear preferences make the labels less useful, creating a practical obstacle for learning from human feedback.

CLARIFY addresses this problem with an offline method that learns a representation of trajectories, or sequences of behavior. Its contrastive learning approach incorporates preference information into an embedding space: a representation in which clearly distinguishable segments are placed apart. This gives the method a basis for selecting comparisons that are less ambiguous for the person providing feedback.

The reported experiments show CLARIFY outperforming baselines in settings involving both non-ideal teachers and real human feedback. The findings also indicate that it selects more distinguishable queries and learns meaningful trajectory representations. These results connect the representation-learning step to the feedback problem: organizing behavior using preference information can help identify comparisons that people can judge more clearly.
icml-2025-clarify-contrastive-preference.tldr: CLARIFY learns preference-informed representations of behavior to select less ambiguous comparisons, outperforming baselines in experiments with non-ideal teachers and real human feedback.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods explore by introducing randomness into actions or policy parameters, yet deployment often calls for a deterministic policy. Existing convergence guarantees typically keep this randomness fixed at a level chosen for the desired final accuracy. This paper analyzes approaches that change stochasticity during training, as practitioners commonly do.

The first method, PES, divides learning into phases. Each phase runs policy gradient with fixed stochasticity, and a deterministic schedule reduces that stochasticity between phases. Under gradient domination assumptions, the authors prove convergence of the final iterate to an optimal deterministic policy. Its sample complexity scales as approximately epsilon to the power minus five, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

The paper also studies SL-PG, which jointly learns policy parameters and stochasticity through an appropriate parameterization. Under stronger assumptions, it achieves last-iterate convergence at a rate of approximately epsilon to the power minus three. Its guarantee concerns an optimal stochastic policy or hyperpolicy, however. The two results establish different trade-offs: PES targets deterministic optimality, while the stronger-assumption SL-PG analysis guarantees stochastic optimality.
icml-2025-convergence-analysis-of-policy.tldr: The paper proves distinct convergence guarantees for scheduled stochasticity reduction and jointly learned stochasticity in policy gradient methods.

paragraphs: Weighted Euclidean distance lets different coordinates contribute differently to a distance calculation. When weights are known in advance, dimensionality reduction can first scale the coordinates and then apply a standard distance-preserving projection. This familiar recipe does not directly address weights that are revealed later or change after the vectors have been compressed.

The paper constructs a linear map from real vectors into a smaller complex vector space. The resulting representation supports a Johnson–Lindenstrauss-like estimate of weighted Euclidean distance once the weights become available. This moves the choice of weights beyond the initial compression step, addressing the dynamic-weight setting directly.

The theoretical analysis decomposes the complex projection into random quantities called Rademacher chaoses. The authors develop new concentration inequalities for sums of independent quantities of this kind to establish their result. These inequalities control random variation in the construction and underpin the distance estimate. The contribution is both a dimensionality-reduction method for deferred weighting and probability tools supporting its guarantees.
icml-2025-dimensionality-reduction-on-co.tldr: A projection into a smaller complex space enables JL-like weighted distance estimates even when weights are revealed after compression.

paragraphs: DISCO predicts how a dynamical system will evolve from a short observed trajectory, without knowing the temporal partial differential equations governing it. The paper draws on a useful property of numerical simulation: when the governing evolution rule is known, a relatively compact solver can advance the system through time.

The architecture separates discovering that rule from using it. A large hypernetwork reads the short trajectory and generates parameters for a much smaller operator network. The operator network then predicts subsequent states through time integration. This division gives the large model responsibility for estimating dynamics and the smaller model responsibility for repeatedly evolving the state.

Experiments show that pretraining across diverse physics datasets produces state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer training epochs. The model also generalizes well to unseen initial conditions and remains competitive after fine-tuning on downstream tasks. These findings support separating dynamics estimation from state prediction as a useful architectural choice for learning across physical systems whose governing equations are unavailable.
icml-2025-disco-learning-to-discover-an-.tldr: DISCO uses a large hypernetwork to infer a compact evolution operator from a short trajectory, enabling efficient prediction of unknown physical dynamics.

paragraphs: Models of molecular and physical systems need to account for geometry across an entire structure while responding consistently to rotations and translations. Equivariant self-attention can provide global context, but its quadratic complexity makes large systems expensive. Local message passing reduces that burden while giving up global information.

Geometric Hyena introduces an equivariant architecture based on long convolutions, inspired by state-space and long-convolution models. It captures global geometric context with sub-quadratic complexity and preserves equivariance to rotations and translations. The design addresses global interaction modeling and geometric consistency within the same scalable architecture.

The authors evaluate it on all-atom property prediction for large RNA molecules and full protein molecular dynamics. They report stronger performance than existing equivariant models and substantially lower memory and compute requirements than equivariant self-attention. In the reported comparison, it processes 30,000 tokens of geometric context 20 times faster than an equivariant transformer and supports 72 times longer context within the same budget. These results demonstrate practical gains for the evaluated large molecular systems.
icml-2025-geometric-hyena-networks-for-l.tldr: Geometric Hyena uses equivariant long convolutions to model global geometry with sub-quadratic complexity and strong reported molecular-task performance.

paragraphs: As text-to-video systems improve, evaluating their outputs requires understanding what a video depicts and whether its events make sense. The paper identifies a gap between human judgment and automated metrics that lack high-level semantic reasoning. Its goal is to produce assessments that include explanations alongside scores.

The authors construct GRADEO-Instruct, an instruction-tuning dataset covering multiple evaluation dimensions. It contains 3,300 videos from more than ten generation models, with multi-step reasoning assessments derived from 16,000 human annotations. They then introduce GRADEO, a model designed specifically to evaluate generated videos through multi-step reasoning.

Experiments show that GRADEO’s assessments align more closely with human evaluations than existing methods. Its benchmarking also reveals difficulties among current video generators in producing content consistent with human reasoning and complex real-world situations. The work therefore contributes both an evaluator and evidence about generation weaknesses. Its reported advantage concerns agreement with human judgments, while its explanatory assessments make the basis of a score more accessible.
icml-2025-gradeo-towards-human-like-eval.tldr: GRADEO uses human-derived multi-step assessments to evaluate generated videos with explanations and closer agreement with human judgments.

paragraphs: Production lines often need ongoing decisions about routing, worker allocation, and scheduling to maintain performance. Reinforcement learning offers a way to learn such control policies, but research lacks a standardized general framework for developing and comparing them. LineFlow supplies an extensible, open-source Python environment for this purpose.

The framework simulates production lines of arbitrary complexity and supports training reinforcement learning agents to control them. To establish reference points, the authors formulate core control subproblems in mathematically analyzable forms and provide optimal solutions. These solutions make it possible to compare learned behavior with a known target in well-understood settings.

Benchmarks show that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms can learn policies approaching optimal performance in those settings. More complex, industrial-scale lines remain substantially harder. The authors identify reward shaping, curriculum learning, and hierarchical control as areas needing further research. LineFlow therefore contributes a common experimental foundation and demonstrates both the promise of learned production control and the challenges encountered as line complexity increases.
icml-2025-lineflow-a-framework-to-learn-.tldr: LineFlow provides production-line simulation and RL training, showing near-optimal control in simpler settings and persistent challenges at industrial scale.

paragraphs: Mahalanobis-based detectors identify unfamiliar inputs using features from just before a neural network’s output layer. These post-hoc methods can perform well at ImageNet scale, yet their effectiveness varies considerably between models. This paper links that inconsistency to large differences in the lengths, or norms, of feature vectors.

The distance estimation relies on a Gaussian modeling assumption with a shared covariance matrix. Strong norm variation can severely violate that assumption. The authors show that applying l2 normalization to features mitigates the problem and makes the representation better aligned with the modeling premise. The proposed change is therefore a simple transformation of the features used by the detector.

Experiments across 44 models, covering diverse architectures and pretraining schemes, show substantial and consistent improvements over conventional Mahalanobis approaches. The normalized method also outperforms other recently proposed OOD detectors in the reported evaluations. The findings connect a practical performance issue to a mismatch in feature geometry and show that a small preprocessing change can improve this family of detectors.
icml-2025-mahalanobis-improving-ood-dete.tldr: Normalizing feature vectors substantially improves Mahalanobis OOD detection across 44 evaluated models by mitigating problematic feature-norm variation.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability methods aim to identify how neural networks carry out tasks, but comparing their progress requires shared evaluation standards. MIB introduces a benchmark spanning four tasks and five models. It rewards explanations that recover relevant causal pathways or variables precisely and concisely.

The benchmark has two tracks. Circuit localization evaluates methods that identify important model components and their connections. Causal variable localization evaluates methods that turn hidden vectors into features and align those features with task-relevant causal variables. This separates finding where a computation happens from identifying the variables represented within that computation.

On MIB, attribution and mask optimization methods perform best at circuit localization. The supervised distributed alignment search method performs best at causal variable localization, while sparse autoencoder features do not outperform neurons in that track. These are findings within the benchmark’s tasks and models. They provide concrete comparisons among interpretability approaches and show how a shared evaluation can distinguish improvements in different aspects of causal explanation.
icml-2025-mib-a-mechanistic-interpretabi.tldr: MIB benchmarks causal circuit and variable localization, revealing distinct strengths among interpretability methods across four tasks and five models.

paragraphs: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem concerns coloring the plane so that points one unit apart never share a color. It combines continuous geometry with discrete color choices and hard constraints. This paper uses that setting to demonstrate how neural networks can assist mathematical discovery by exploring possible configurations.

The authors use neural networks as approximators and reformulate the coloring task through a probabilistic, differentiable loss. This makes gradient-based optimization available for exploring admissible colorings. The central methodological contribution is a way to bring a constrained geometric search into a form that neural optimization can investigate.

The approach led to two new six-colorings, producing the first improvement in thirty years for an off-diagonal variant of the original problem. The result concerns that variant, rather than a resolution of the original Hadwiger–Nelson problem. This paper establishes the machine learning approach behind those discoveries and presents additional numerical insights demonstrating broader applicability. Its significance is a concrete connection between differentiable search and new mathematical constructions.
icml-2025-neural-discovery-in-mathematic.tldr: A differentiable neural formulation of geometric coloring helped discover two six-colorings that improve an off-diagonal Hadwiger–Nelson variant.

paragraphs: Standard reinforcement learning often evaluates a policy through a linear objective over the states and actions it visits. This paper studies episodic, finite-horizon problems with convex losses on that visitation distribution. The setting, called concave utility reinforcement learning, allows nonlinear objectives but invalidates the classical Bellman equations used by many RL methods.

The authors introduce an algorithm with near-optimal online regret bounds despite having no prior knowledge of the environment’s transition function. It combines online mirror descent with changing constraint sets and a carefully constructed exploration bonus. These elements support learning both how to act and how the unknown environment evolves.

The paper also studies a bandit version in which feedback consists only of the objective’s value on the distribution induced by the chosen policy. By adapting bandit convex optimization techniques to Markov decision processes, the authors obtain sublinear regret for this more restrictive feedback setting. The results establish learning guarantees for nonlinear policy objectives under both unknown dynamics and limited feedback.
icml-2025-online-episodic-convex-reinfor.tldr: New online algorithms achieve regret guarantees for convex RL objectives with unknown dynamics, including a version with only objective-value feedback.

paragraphs: Long mathematical reasoning chains can be difficult to check because a step may depend on statements much earlier in the solution. This paper makes those dependencies explicit. Its starting observation is that a mathematical step can be derived from a small set of premises drawn from preceding steps.

Premise Augmented Reasoning Chains, or PARC, add links from each step to its supporting premises. The resulting representation is a directed acyclic graph: steps become nodes, and premise dependencies become edges. Verification can then examine a step together with the particular statements it relies on, making the relevant context directly available.

Using a dataset built for premise and error identification, the authors show that language models can reliably identify premises in complex chains. Even open-source models achieve 90% premise-identification recall in the reported experiments. Checking steps under their linked premises improves error-identification accuracy by 6 to 16 percentage points. These findings support dependency-aware representations as a practical way to improve the evaluation of mathematical reasoning.
icml-2025-premise-augmented-reasoning-ch.tldr: Linking mathematical reasoning steps to their premises improves reported error-identification accuracy by 6 to 16 percentage points.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization trains a stronger model using labels from a weaker model, hoping the student can outperform its supervisor. Previous theory for squared-loss regression relates this performance gain to the mismatch between the two models. This paper extends that relationship to a broader family of learning objectives.

The authors establish a misfit-based characterization for losses corresponding to arbitrary Bregman divergences, assuming the strong model class is convex. Because cross-entropy can be expressed through a Bregman divergence, the result reaches classification as well as regression. The convexity assumption is central to this part of the theory.

To address strong model classes that are not convex, the authors study convex combinations of k strong models in classification. They obtain a similar characterization with an extra error term that vanishes as k grows. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The work broadens the conditions under which disagreement with a weak supervisor can quantitatively explain a stronger model’s performance gain.
icml-2025-relating-misfit-to-gain-in-wea.tldr: The paper extends misfit-based weak-to-strong performance theory to Bregman losses and classification, with convexity assumptions or mixtures of strong models.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can search complex structured domains, such as valid molecules, through the latent space of a variational autoencoder. Existing approaches tightly connect the generative model with a surrogate that predicts candidate quality. That coupling can perform poorly when the latent space is not well suited to the particular optimization task.

This paper proposes training the two components separately. The variational autoencoder focuses on generating structures, while a Gaussian process surrogate focuses on predictive modeling. A Bayesian update rule then combines them. The design gives each model a distinct role while providing a principled mechanism for bringing their information together.

The authors show that this decoupled approach improves the identification of promising candidates in molecular optimization under constrained evaluation budgets. That setting makes candidate selection especially consequential because only a limited number of evaluations are available. The reported findings support separating generation and prediction as an effective design choice for these tasks, without requiring increasingly elaborate coupling between the models.
icml-2025-return-of-the-latent-space-cow.tldr: Separately training a VAE and Gaussian process, then combining them through Bayesian updating, improves molecular candidate selection under limited evaluation budgets.

paragraphs: GFlowNets generate objects by sampling construction trajectories through an environment graph. Their target distribution may be specified only up to a normalizing constant. Much of the usual theory relies on acyclic graphs, where trajectories cannot return to earlier states. This paper revisits the theory for discrete environments that allow cycles.

The authors present a simpler framework for these non-acyclic GFlowNets. They develop results concerning training with fixed backward policies, the properties of flow functions, and connections to entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. These results extend concepts from the acyclic setting into a broader class of environments, providing a more unified theoretical account.

The paper also experimentally re-examines loss stability in non-acyclic training and validates its own theoretical findings. Its contribution is therefore both conceptual and empirical: it clarifies how the framework behaves when cycles are present and tests aspects of that account. This matters for understanding which familiar GFlowNet ideas can carry over once the acyclicity assumption is relaxed.
icml-2025-revisiting-non-acyclic-gflowne.tldr: A simpler theory for discrete GFlowNets with cycles extends flow, backward-policy, and entropy-regularized RL results beyond acyclic environments.

paragraphs: Compressing language models can reduce memory use and accelerate inference, but preserving accuracy often requires expensive retraining. SLIM combines quantization, sparsity, and low-rank approximation in a one-shot process. Its aim is to manage the errors from these compression steps together while using hardware-friendly representations.

First, a probabilistic formulation enables uniform weight quantization. An existing one-shot pruning method then introduces semi-structured sparsity. Finally, a saliency function with invertible and additive properties allows the method to calculate low-rank adapters that compensate for the combined quantization and pruning error. The adapters address the accumulated distortion from both earlier stages.

For LLaMA-2-7B with 4-bit weights and 2:4 sparsity, the authors report accuracy improvements of up to 5.66% over prior methods. They also report performance speedups reaching 4.3 times on RTX3060 and 3.8 times on A100 GPUs, alongside reduced memory use. An optional parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipe improves accuracy by up to another 1.66% for LLaMA-2-13B relative to SLIM without fine-tuning. That optional step is separate from the core one-shot process.
icml-2025-slim-one-shot-quantization-and.tldr: SLIM jointly manages quantization and pruning error with computed low-rank adapters, improving reported accuracy and inference efficiency without core-method retraining.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns a representation of the environment and predicts how it changes. Such a world model can support learning through imagined rollouts, while its representation also becomes input to the agent’s behavior model. SOLD studies the value of organizing that representation around objects and their interactions.

The method uses slot attention to learn object-centric latent dynamics from pixels without supervision. Instead of encoding the whole scene only as a holistic state, its structured latent space represents the environment in an object-focused way. The authors show that this improves model interpretability and gives behavior models a useful space for relational reasoning.

Across multi-object manipulation environments requiring both relational reasoning and dexterous control, SOLD outperforms DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 in the reported results. These comparisons support the usefulness of object-centric dynamics for the evaluated control tasks. The broader motivation is that a world model’s internal organization matters twice: for predicting environmental changes and for providing information that helps the agent learn how to act.
icml-2025-sold-slot-object-centric-laten.tldr: SOLD learns object-centric world models from pixels and outperforms DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 on evaluated relational manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: HypotheSAEs generates interpretable hypotheses about relationships between text and a target variable, such as headline content and clicks. The aim is to find patterns that both predict an outcome and can be expressed in ordinary language, making them useful candidates for further investigation.

The method has three stages. A sparse autoencoder learns interpretable features from text embeddings. Features that predict the target variable are then selected. Finally, a language model describes each selected feature in natural language. Those descriptions become hypotheses about what predicts the target, connecting statistical feature selection with human-readable explanations.

On synthetic datasets, the method improves recovery of reference hypotheses by at least 0.06 F1 over baselines. On real datasets, it produces twice as many significant findings while using one to two orders of magnitude less compute than recent LLM-based approaches. The authors also report new discoveries concerning partisan differences in Congressional speeches and engagement with online headlines. These are hypotheses about predictive relationships; the method’s stated goal is to identify interpretable associations.
icml-2025-sparse-autoencoders-for-hypoth.tldr: HypotheSAEs turns predictive sparse-autoencoder features into readable hypotheses, reporting stronger discoveries with much less compute than recent LLM-based methods.

paragraphs: Structured Kernel Interpolation makes Gaussian processes more scalable by approximating their kernel matrix through interpolation at inducing points. Although this can enable linear computational complexity, understanding the approximation’s accuracy requires explicit error analysis. This paper supplies bounds for the approximated Gram matrix and studies their effects on hyperparameter estimation and posterior inference.

For convolutional cubic interpolation, the analysis recommends growing the number of inducing points as n to the power d/3, where n is sample size and d is dimension. This connects a practical approximation choice to error control and shows how strongly the required resources depend on dimensionality.

The authors distinguish two regimes for spectral-norm error and computational complexity. When d is below three, any error tolerance can be achieved in linear time for sufficiently large sample sizes. When d is at least three, their guarantees require error to increase with sample size. This higher-dimensional statement describes the limits of the supplied guarantees. The analysis makes the accuracy–scalability trade-off explicit and identifies conditions supporting controlled-error, linear-time inference.
icml-2025-the-price-of-linear-time-error.tldr: SKI error bounds reveal dimension-dependent conditions for combining controlled approximation error with linear-time Gaussian process inference.
